prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

ISLAMABAD, Pakistan (CNN) -- Pakistan's foreign ministry said Wednesday that it has lodged a "strong" protest with the U.S. ambassador over missile attacks conducted on Pakistani soil by unmanned drones. The aftermath of a suspected U.S. drone attack on a building in North Waziristan. The ministry said it summoned Ambassador Anne Patterson to underscore that such attacks violate Pakistan's sovereignty and should be stopped immediately. A statement from the ministry said Patterson was also told that the attacks have cost lives and undermined public support for Pakistan's counter terrorism efforts. The ministry lodged its protests three days after a missile strike from a suspected U.S. drone on a compound in South Waziristan killed 20 people. Pakistan has repeatedly raised objections to foreign nations violating its sovereignty to pursue terrorists. A U.S. ground operation in September that left several civilians dead rankled relations between the two countries. Last week, Pakistan's parliament passed a resolution that condemned any incursion on Pakistani soil by foreign forces. The resolution called for a review of the country's national security strategy and said the government needs to safeguard its sovereignty and territorial integrity. The ministry said it handed Patterson a copy of the resolution. The U.S. and NATO, which have troops in Afghanistan, have been seeking a way to effectively battle militants who launch attacks from Pakistan's swath of tribal areas along the border. They have become frustrated with Islamabad over the years, saying it is not being proactive enough against militants -- a claim Pakistan denies. The United States is the only country operating in the region known to have the capability to launch missiles from drones, which are controlled remotely. In another development, suspected Taliban militants kidnapped three government officials from an administrative office in Pakistan's tribal region Wednesday, officials said. The militants abducted two employees and a security guard from the Ambar district in Mohmand Agency. Mohmand is in the Federally Administered Tribal Areas, where U.S. and Pakistani officials have reported a presence of militants. Earlier in the day, militants tried unsuccessfully to take control of a school in Mohmand and abduct about 100 students, authorities said. A shootout with Frontier Corps followed, in which one militant was killed and another arrested. The Frontier Corps is a paramilitary force which uses recruits from Pakistan's tribal areas and is overseen by Pakistani army officers. Also Wednesday, a suicide car bomber detonated explosives outside a police checkpoint in northwest Pakistan, killing two security personnel, officials said. The Wednesday afternoon attack in the Bannu district of the North West Frontier Province also wounded a dozen people, military sources said. The bomber targeted a check point near a military hospital, said the sources who did not want their names revealed because they are not authorized to speak to the media. CNN's Reza Sayah and journalist Janullah Hashimzada contributed to this report .

Ambassador Anne Patterson was called to the ministry and informed that the attacks breached Pakistan’s sovereignty and must end at once. Ministry officials also told her that the strikes had caused deaths and weakened public backing for Pakistan’s counterterrorism campaign. The ministry provided Patterson with a copy of a parliamentary resolution addressing the issue.

The diplomatic protest came three days after 20 people were killed when a missile, believed to have been launched by a U.S. unmanned aircraft, struck a compound in South Waziristan. Another suspected U.S. drone strike had previously targeted a building in North Waziristan.

Pakistan has repeatedly objected to foreign countries entering its territory while pursuing suspected terrorists. Relations with Washington were strained further in September after a U.S. ground operation resulted in the deaths of several civilians.

The previous week, Pakistan’s Parliament approved a resolution denouncing any entry into the country by foreign forces. It also urged a reassessment of the national security strategy and called on the government to protect Pakistan’s sovereignty and territorial integrity.

The United States and NATO, whose forces are stationed in Afghanistan, have been trying to find an effective way to combat militants who use Pakistan’s tribal belt along the Afghan border as a base for attacks. Over the years, they have expressed frustration with Islamabad, accusing it of failing to act aggressively enough against the militants. Pakistan rejects that allegation.

Among countries operating in the area, only the United States is known to possess the ability to fire missiles from remotely controlled drones.

In a separate incident Wednesday, suspected Taliban fighters seized three government workers from an administrative office in Pakistan’s tribal region, according to officials. Two employees and a security guard were taken from Ambar district in Mohmand Agency.

Mohmand lies within the Federally Administered Tribal Areas, where both Pakistani and U.S. officials have said militants are active.

Earlier that day, militants attempted but failed to capture a school in Mohmand and kidnap roughly 100 students, authorities reported. A gunbattle with the Frontier Corps followed, leaving one militant dead and another in custody.

The Frontier Corps is a paramilitary organization staffed by recruits from Pakistan’s tribal regions and supervised by officers from the Pakistani army.

Also on Wednesday, a suicide attacker detonated a vehicle packed with explosives outside a police checkpoint in northwestern Pakistan. Officials said two members of the security forces were killed.

Military sources reported that 12 additional people were injured in the afternoon bombing in Bannu district, located in the North West Frontier Province. The attacker struck a checkpoint close to a military hospital, according to sources who requested anonymity because they were not permitted to speak publicly.

Patterson was summoned to the ministry and told that the missile attacks violated Pakistan’s sovereignty and risked undermining public support for counterterrorism operations. Pakistani officials have repeatedly objected to suspected U.S. drone strikes in the tribal belt, even as Washington has pressed Islamabad to act against al Qaeda and Taliban militants using the region as a sanctuary.

The United States generally does not publicly confirm individual drone operations. U.S. officials have maintained that militants based near the Afghan border pose a threat to American and NATO forces in Afghanistan.

The diplomatic confrontation came amid a series of security incidents in northwest Pakistan. Militants carried out kidnappings in the region, targeting people they believed could be used as bargaining chips, according to local authorities. Security forces launched searches, but the rugged terrain and the presence of armed groups complicated rescue efforts.

Separately, a suicide bomber struck in the northwest, killing and wounding civilians and security personnel, officials said. Investigators were working to determine which militant organization was responsible.

Pakistan’s tribal areas and neighboring districts have seen repeated bombings, abductions and clashes since the government stepped up operations against Islamist militants. The violence has also fueled tensions between Washington and Islamabad, whose cooperation is considered critical to the campaign against al Qaeda and the Taliban.

**U.S.-Pakistan tensions rise after drone strike kills 20 in South Waziristan**

*Pakistan condemns attack as violation of sovereignty; lawmakers demand halt to cross-border strikes as separate Taliban-related violence unsettles tribal areas*

**ISLAMABAD, Pakistan —** Tensions between the United States and Pakistan rose sharply after a suspected U.S. drone strike killed at least 20 people in South Waziristan, Pakistani officials said, intensifying anger over Washington’s use of unmanned aircraft inside Pakistani territory.

The strike hit a suspected militant compound in the tribal district near the Afghan border, according to local officials and residents. Intelligence officials said militants were believed to be among the dead, but the identities of those killed—and whether civilians were among them—could not immediately be independently verified. The United States did not immediately acknowledge carrying out the attack.

Pakistan’s government condemned the strike as a violation of the country’s sovereignty. Islamabad has repeatedly warned that unilateral attacks undermine public support for counterterrorism operations and fuel anti-American sentiment, even as Washington argues that militant sanctuaries in the border region pose a direct threat to U.S. and allied forces in Afghanistan.

The attack adds urgency to a parliamentary resolution asserting Pakistan’s territorial integrity and calling for a security strategy based on national consensus. The resolution rejects incursions into Pakistani territory and says the country’s sovereignty must be defended, while also recognizing the need to confront terrorism and militancy through a combination of political engagement, economic development and, where necessary, security operations.

Lawmakers have demanded greater civilian oversight of counterterrorism policy and an end to foreign attacks conducted without Pakistan’s approval. Although the resolution is not necessarily binding on military operations, it carries significant political weight and reflects broad opposition across party lines to U.S. strikes.

Pakistani officials say they have protested the drone campaign through diplomatic and military channels. Washington, however, has grown increasingly concerned about Taliban and al-Qaeda-linked fighters using the rugged tribal belt to plan attacks, train recruits and cross into Afghanistan.

South Waziristan has long been a center of militant activity and a base for factions aligned with the Pakistani Taliban. The mountainous district’s limited government presence and difficult terrain have made casualty claims following drone strikes especially hard to confirm. Militants frequently seal off targeted locations, while journalists and independent investigators face severe restrictions on access.

The drone strike came amid separate Taliban-related incidents elsewhere in the former Federally Administered Tribal Areas, highlighting the instability facing the region. Pakistani security officials reported fresh militant activity, including attacks or threats against local residents and security personnel, while authorities continued operations against Taliban fighters in several districts. **[Insert verified details of the separate incidents here, including locations, casualty figures and attribution.]**

Those incidents were not directly connected to the South Waziristan strike, but together they underscored the multiple pressures on Islamabad: combating domestic Taliban factions, preventing cross-border infiltration into Afghanistan and resisting foreign military action that is deeply unpopular inside Pakistan.

The United States regards Pakistan as a crucial counterterrorism partner, but drone strikes have repeatedly strained the relationship. Pakistani leaders publicly denounce the attacks, while U.S. officials have maintained that action is necessary when militants operate from areas where local authorities are unable or unwilling to capture them.

Analysts warned that the latest deaths could prompt demonstrations and renewed demands for Pakistan to reconsider security cooperation with Washington. They also said militant groups were likely to exploit the strike for recruitment and propaganda, particularly if reports of civilian casualties emerge.

The full toll and the identities of those killed remained under investigation. Independent confirmation was not immediately possible because access to South Waziristan is tightly restricted and initial accounts from the area often differ.

### Pakistan protests U.S. missile strikes as militant violence spreads

**ISLAMABAD, Nov. 20, 2008** — Pakistan summoned U.S. Ambassador Anne W. Patterson to lodge a formal protest after two suspected American drone strikes hit Pakistani territory the previous day, including an unusual attack in the settled district of Bannu, outside the federally administered tribal areas.

Pakistani officials said the strikes violated the country’s sovereignty and risked civilian casualties. Islamabad also warned that unilateral attacks undermined public support for joint counterterrorism efforts, strengthened anti-American sentiment and complicated cooperation with Washington against al-Qaeda and Taliban militants. The United States generally did not publicly acknowledge individual drone operations, although the campaign was widely attributed to the CIA.

The strikes reportedly targeted suspected militant compounds in the Bannu area of the North West Frontier Province and in North Waziristan. Local accounts said several people were killed, but their identities and any militant affiliations could not be independently confirmed.

The protest illustrated the tension at the center of the U.S.-Pakistan counterterrorism relationship. Washington viewed the tribal belt as a refuge for militants involved in attacks in Afghanistan and elsewhere, while Pakistan argued that repeated cross-border strikes were politically destabilizing and made its own military campaign more difficult. Despite the dispute, intelligence and security cooperation between the two countries continued.

The missile attacks came amid additional militant violence on Wednesday. In the Mohmand tribal region, insurgents attacked a paramilitary position, killing security personnel before government forces returned fire. In the North West Frontier Province, militants also attacked police in the Swat Valley, killing an officer and abducting others, according to local authorities.

Together, the incidents showed that Pakistan was facing pressure from both sides: escalating militant attacks at home and increasingly aggressive U.S. action against suspected militant sanctuaries inside Pakistani territory.
